L244: # Arctic Ice Melt Is Changing Ocean Currents
L245: 
L246: cite166†Image: The headshot image of Anthony Greicius†secure.gravatar.com L247: 
L248: Anthony Greicius
L249: 
L250: Feb 06, 2020
L251: 
L252: Article
L253: Arctic sea ice was photographed in 2011 during NASA’s ICESCAPE mission, or “Impacts of Climate on Ecosystems and Chemistry of the Arctic Pacific Environment,” a shipborne investigation to study how changing conditions in the Arctic affect the ocean’s chemistry and ecosystems. The bulk of the research took place in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas in summer 2010 and 2011.
L254: 
L255: Credits: NASA/Kathryn Hansen
L256: A major ocean current in the Arctic is faster and more turbulent as a result of rapid sea ice melt, a new study from NASA shows. The current is part of a delicate Arctic environment that is now flooded with fresh water, an effect of human-caused climate change.
L257: Using 12 years of satellite data, scientists have measured how this circular current, called the Beaufort Gyre, has precariously balanced an influx of unprecedented amounts of cold, fresh water — a change that could alter the currents in the Atlantic Ocean and cool the climate of Western Europe.
L258: The Beaufort Gyre keeps the polar environment in equilibrium by storing fresh water near the surface of the ocean. Wind blows the gyre in a clockwise direction around the western Arctic Ocean, north of Canada and Alaska, where it naturally collects fresh water from glacial melt, river runoff and precipitation. This fresh water is important in the Arctic in part because it floats above the warmer, salty water and helps to protect the sea ice from melting, which in turn helps regulate Earth’s climate.
L259: The gyre then slowly releases this fresh water into the Atlantic Ocean over a period of decades, allowing the Atlantic Ocean currents to carry it away in small amounts.
L260: But the since the 1990s, the gyre has accumulated a large amount of fresh water — 1,920 cubic miles (8,000 cubic kilometers) — or almost twice the volume of Lake Michigan. The new study, published in Nature Communications, found that the cause of this gain in freshwater concentration is the loss of sea ice in summer and autumn.
L261: This decades-long decline of the Arctic’s summertime sea ice cover has left the Beaufort Gyre more exposed to the wind, which spins the gyre faster and traps the fresh water in its current.
L262: Persistent westerly winds have also dragged the current in one direction for over 20 years, increasing the speed and size of the clockwise current and preventing the fresh water from leaving the Arctic Ocean. This decades-long western wind is unusual for the region, where previously, the winds changed direction every five to seven years.
L263: Scientists have been keeping an eye on the Beaufort Gyre in case the wind changes direction again. If the direction were to change, the wind would reverse the current, pulling it counterclockwise and releasing the water it has accumulated all at once.
L264: “If the Beaufort Gyre were to release the excess fresh water into the Atlantic Ocean, it could potentially slow down its circulation. And that would have hemisphere-wide implications for the climate, especially in Western Europe,” said Tom Armitage, lead author of the study and polar scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California.
L265: Fresh water released from the Arctic Ocean to the North Atlantic can change the density of surface waters. Normally, water from the Arctic loses heat and moisture to the atmosphere and sinks to the bottom of the ocean, where it drives water from the north Atlantic Ocean down to the tropics like a conveyor belt.
L266: This important current is called the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and helps regulate the planet’s climate by carrying heat from the tropically-warmed water to northern latitudes like Europe and North America. If slowed enough, it could negatively impact marine life and the communities that depend on it.
L267: “We don’t expect a shutting down of the Gulf Stream, but we do expect impacts. That’s why we’re monitoring the Beaufort Gyre so closely,” said Alek Petty, a co-author on the paper and polar scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
L268: The study also found that, although the Beaufort Gyre is out of balance because of the added energy from the wind, the current expels that excess energy by forming small, circular eddies of water. While the increased turbulence has helped keep the system balanced, it has the potential to lead to further ice melt because it mixes layers of cold, fresh water with relatively warm, salt water below.
L269: The melting ice could, in turn, lead to changes in how nutrients and organic material in the ocean are mixed, significantly affecting the food chain and wildlife in the Arctic. The results reveal a delicate balance between wind and ocean as the sea ice pack recedes under climate change.
L270: “What this study is showing is that the loss of sea ice has really important impacts on our climate system that we’re only just discovering,” said Petty.

L150@P6: Perennial and Seasonal Ice
L151@P6: The Arctic sea ice cover is composed of perennial ice (the ice that survives year round,
L152@P6: generally located towards the center of the Arctic basin) and seasonal ice (the ice around the
L153@P6: periphery of the Arctic basin that melts during the summer). Consistent with the diminishing
L154@P6: trends in the extent and thickness of the cover is the observation of a significant loss of the
L155@P6: older, thicker perennial ice in the Arctic (Figure I3). Results from a simulation using drifting buoy
L156@P6: data and satellite-derived ice concentration data to estimate the age distribution of ice in the
L157@P6: Arctic Basin (Rigor and Wallace, 2004) indicate that the March ice cover has experienced a
L158@P6: significant decline in the relative amount of perennial ice over the period 1958-2006, from
L159@P6: approximately 5.5 million km2
L160@P6:  to 3.0 million km2. While there is significant interannual variability,
L161@P6: a generally downward trend in the amount of perennial ice begins in the early 1970s. This trend
L162@P6: appears to coincide with a general increase in the Arctic-wide, annually averaged surface air
L163@P6: temperature, which also begins around 1970 (Figure A2).

L218@P9: Surface circulation regime
L219@P9: The circulation of the sea ice cover and ocean surface layer are closely coupled and are
L220@P9: primarily wind-driven (Proshutinsky and Johnson, 1997). Data from satellites and drifting buoys
L221@P9: indicate that the entire period of 2000-2006 has been characterized by an anticyclonic
L222@P9: (clockwise) circulation regime due to a higher sea level atmospheric pressure over the region
L223@P9: north of Alaska, relative to the 1948-2005 mean, and the prevalence of anticyclonic winds
L224@P9: (Figure O1). Under these conditions, the clockwise circulation pattern in the Beaufort Sea region
L225@P9: (the Beaufort Gyre) tends to be relatively strong. Conversely, in the cyclonic regime the
L226@P9: clockwise circulation pattern in the Beaufort Sea region weakens, and the flow across the basin,
L227@P9: from the Siberian and Russian coasts to Fram Strait (the Transpolar Drift), shifts poleward. The
L228@P9: cyclonic pattern dominated during 1989-1996; the anticyclonic pattern has prevailed since 1997.
L229@P9: The dominance of the anticyclonic regime during last decade of 1997-2006 is consistent with
L230@P9: the Arctic Oscillation (AO) index (Figure A1) which fluctuated about zero indicating a relatively
L231@P9: low level of influence from the Atlantic on these Arctic processes (Rigor et al., 2002).
L232@P9: Figure O1. Sea ice drift pattern (arrows) in October-May 2000-2006 and sea
L233@P9: surface atmospheric pressure distribution. Sea level atmospheric pressure is
L234@P9: shown by lines (hPa) (courtesy of Ron Kwok).

L17: # Sea ice around Iceland
L18: Ice in the ocean around Iceland has mostly arrived from afar. It comes from the Denmark strait, which connects the Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic Ocean, between Iceland and Greenland. Sometimes the ice comes directly from north to the northeast corner of Iceland, but all the ice comes from the same source: The East-Greenland current which flows from the Arctic Ocean due south along the east coast of Greenland, passing northwest Iceland.
L19: This great cold current transports a lot of ice southwards, both sea ice which is formed in sea water and ice bergs which break off from the glacier of Greenland.
L20: Late winter the ice can cover fishing grounds northwest of Iceland. This ice is often carried eastwards, into the pathways of ships along the Icelandic coast and sometimes into fjords and bays. Ice bergs are also seen around Iceland, especially in autumn.
L21: Whether ice comes close to Iceland depends on three factors: The quantity of ice in Denmark strait, the condition in the ocean near Iceland, i.e. temperature, salinity and layering, and the overall air circulation in the northern hemisphere, i.e. lows and highs, especially the development of static high pressure over either Greenland or the Atlantic Ocean.

L28: A combination of certain circumstances causes the long dreaded "hafis" which meant very cold winters and harsh living in earlier centuries. Sometimes loss of lifestock and local starvation followed, though rarely.
L29: Contrarily, ice on the Icelandic fishing grounds is quite common, especially in the northwest. Therefore, sea ice is monitored by regular flights for this purpose. Based on cite5†observations from the Icelandic Coast Guard and other vessels that sight sea ice, warnings are issued by IMO when considered necessary. The Danish Meteorological Institute produces weekly cite6†maps showing the extent†www.vedur.is of ice dispersion.
